o1.biggest_strength: Every kill, scale and day-30 rule is converted into dollars from the $38 90-day payback, and the day-30 test checks TikTok's new customers against Meta held flat, so it can't take credit for Meta's orders.
o1.biggest_mistake: It uses 'new customers vs prior 30 days' as a pass test but never tells the team to record that baseline in week 0, and it sets an unexplained 21+ age floor that cuts 18-20 buyers for no reason in the data.
o1.what_would_make_it_a_10: Add a recorded pre-launch baseline (new customers a day, blended cost per new customer) and a spend-per-ad floor so the kill and scale calls are provably powered, and drop the arbitrary 21+ floor.

o2.biggest_strength: It does the maths a real buyer does before spending: $114 to judge an ad, $136 minimum per ad group, first-order payback only at $27.10, and store orders rather than TikTok's number decide every call.
o2.biggest_mistake: The handoff is thinner than the analysis: no comment moderation, no ad-review lead time, no named day-to-day owner for kill and scale calls, and month 2 spend after a pass is left vague.
o2.what_would_make_it_a_10: Close the operational gaps - comments owner, upload-by deadline, named kill/scale owner, and a concrete month-2 budget after a pass - while keeping the statistical floors and the verbatim customer hooks.

reason: Both get the money right and both would run, but Output 1 is the one I can actually hand over on Monday: named owners, a week-0 checklist that ends in proven test orders, upload deadlines, comment cover and a stated month-2 budget for pass, hold and fail. Output 2 is the sharper piece of analysis, but it leaves the everyday running of the account under-specified.
